You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the background into a basketball court
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image show a basketball court as the background, with recognizable court features such as a playing surface and court markings or basketball equipment?
node.criteria: Pass if the background is visibly a basketball court with recognizable court features. Fail if the background is clearly not a basketball court. Unknown if the background or its features cannot be assessed reliably.
node.binding: The requested outcome is to replace the image background with a basketball court; judge the edited image against that outcome.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a basketball court background, including a hoop and net, basketballs, and visible court markings on the playing surface.

fulfillment: The node already agrees with the reference and its evidence is strongly supported by the edited image: the kitchen is replaced by a basketball-court setting with a hoop, balls, and court markings. No semantic change is indicated. For robustness, keep completion tied to the requested background itself and distinguish a clearly complete court from merely court-like partial progress; do not treat the second support’s caveat alone as proof of incompleteness when the image shows the requested features. Preserve unresolved outcomes when visual evidence is genuinely insufficient.
s2: The node’s progress-only framing conflicts with the rubric’s yes criterion: yes means the requested edit is complete, while partial progress is not yes. Here the edited image visibly replaces the kitchen with a basketball-court scene, including a hoop, balls, and court markings; the trace’s “not fully complete” caveat is not supported by a clear remaining kitchen/background area. Align the decision criterion with completion of the requested background, and reserve partial-progress status for discernible but genuinely incomplete replacement. Keep unknown for insufficient visual evidence, not merely because the scene is stylized or confidence varies. The current trace agrees with the reference, so avoid changing the outcome based on the caveat alone.
